threads.body: The new pipelining path skips the standard unopened-port tests, including the callback/context case, even though connection failures are part of the behavior this PR adds and the existing non-pipelining client runs these tests. This also leaves the pre-`generateRequest()` failure path uncovered, where no `PipeliningRequestState` has started a span yet. Please enable this option and ensure both failure variants emit and end the expected per-request span.

[General] The agent calls the application's producer here even when Apache never does. Apache rejects a null target before it touches any producer, so this fallback alone explains the one `generateRequest()` call that `directProducerSynchronousFailureCreatesSpan` observes. `HttpAsyncRequestProducer` gives no side-effect-free contract, so enabling the agent runs user code for a request Apache never generated. Leaving an unstarted state without a span, and calling `disableTestConnectionFailure()`, keeps the agent out of that path.

replies.body: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/http/http-spans/#http-client-span-duration isn't too strict about when the span should be ended. This is because the integration points provided by the clients are different, the requirements in spec shouldn't make instrumentation impossible. This means that ignoring the close failures would be fine, the failures that happen during the actual http request are more interesting. Though, I guess this is fine too.

threads.body: wouldn't it be easier to end the span before calling delegate?

A checked `IOException` from `delegate.close()` bypasses this catch. Because the `finally` block then ends any state that already has a response with `exception == null`, that span is permanently recorded as successful even though consumer cleanup failed (the later aggregate failure cannot amend it because `end()` is idempotent). Catch the checked close failure here as well so it is recorded on the span.

replies.body:
The `IOException` does bypass the `catch (RuntimeException)`, but it does not cause a later aggregate failure.

`PipeliningClientExchangeHandlerImpl.responseCompleted()` handles the two exception types differently:

- An `IOException` from `responseConsumer.close()` is caught and logged by Apache. Processing then continues and the aggregate future is completed with the response result.
- A `RuntimeException` reaches the outer catch block, invokes `failed(ex)`, and fails the aggregate future.

I also verified this behavior directly with HttpAsyncClient 4.1.5: when `close()` threw an `IOException`, `Future.get()` still returned the `200` response and the callback was invoked through `completed()`.

For that reason, the current `finally` behavior is intentional. A checked close exception that Apache suppresses should not replace the response-consumer outcome or turn a caller-visible successful request into an error span. The existing `catch (RuntimeException)` remains necessary because that exception does fail the aggregate future and must be recorded before the idempotent state is ended.

Catching `IOException` and passing it to `state.end()` would make the client span report an error while the Apache future and callback report success, so I would keep the current implementation unchanged.

Apache 4.1.x source: https://apache.googlesource.com/httpasyncclient/+/4.1.x/httpasyncclient/src/main/java/org/apache/http/impl/nio/client/PipeliningClientExchangeHandlerImpl.java#289
